query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a graded interlayer that is a Cu‐enriched high entropy alloy (HEA) between a copper matrix and a conventional refractory HEA coating will improve interfacial adhesion by reducing lattice mismatch and differences in thermal expansion, thereby enhancing wear resistance and surface protection.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) matrix with a clean, pre-treated surface that is ready for deposition.
generation.intervention: Deposit a Cu-rich graded interlayer onto the Cu substrate using a method such as DC-magnetron sputtering (with conditions that promote interdiffusion), then deposit the conventional refractory HEA coating on top.
generation.conditions: Deposition and subsequent annealing under controlled temperature conditions to facilitate a gradual compositional transition. The process should ensure moderate thermal cycling and mechanical loading that are representative of operational wear environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded interlayer provides a compositional—and therefore structural—transition that minimizes abrupt changes in lattice parameters and thermal expansion coefficients between pure Cu and the refractory HEA coating.
generation.mechanism: By gradually transitioning the composition from Cu to the HEA, the graded layer reduces interfacial stresses and bonding discontinuities. This mediates the mismatch challenges and helps prevent delamination while maintaining high wear resistance under mechanical and thermal loads.
generation.predicted_outcome: The improved interfacial bonding will result in enhanced adhesion strength of the coating, reducing delamination during wear tests and improving the overall durability of the surface protection system.
generation.baseline: Direct deposition of the conventional refractory HEA coating on a Cu matrix, which typically results in poor adhesion due to mismatches in lattice structure and thermal expansion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold true under typical surface engineering conditions (such as moderate to high thermal and mechanical stresses); however, extreme oxidizing environments or very high thermal gradients may require further optimization.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal composition gradient of the interlayer, the precise deposition/annealing parameters, and the long-term stability of the interface under cyclic loading still need to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Cu substrates: Group A receives a direct deposition of the refractory HEA coating, while Group B is first coated with a Cu-rich graded interlayer and then with the HEA coating. Subject both groups to identical wear and thermal cycling tests.
measurements: Quantitative adhesion strength via peel or shear tests
Wear rate using standardized tribological testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with the graded interlayer (Group B) do not show a statistically significant improvement in adhesion strength and wear resistance or exhibit similar interfacial defects (e.g., delamination) compared to the direct deposition samples (Group A), then the hypothesis is falsified.

Research has proved that RHEAs have excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, even surpassing the widely used nickel-based alloy [ [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. RHEAs, with excellent mechanical properties at elevated temperatures, are considered promising high-temperature application materials, which are suitable for complex working conditions such as atomic energy, aerospace, the military industry, advanced nuclear reactors, etc. Previous studies focused on mechanical properties at high- and room-temperatures, but with little research and analysis on high-temperature oxidation resistance [ [7] , [8] , [9] ]. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr 2 Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO 4 -VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H 2 SO 4 solution. frame.system: A copper (Cu) matrix intended to be surface‐modified with a wear‐resistant layer (potentially a high entropy alloy or an associated coating system).
frame.goal: To improve the surface wear resistance and protection of the Cu substrate by applying a material that adheres well and imparts high wear resistance.
frame.limitation: Finding a material that not only provides excellent wear resistance but also forms a robust, chemically and structurally compatible bond with the Cu matrix.
root_cause_cues: adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix
constraints: The coating or adhered material must bond strongly to copper.
It must have properties (e.g., similar crystal structure or thermal expansion characteristics) that prevent delamination under service conditions.
It should provide or maintain excellent wear resistance to complement the Cu substrate.
frame.regime: Surface engineering conditions (e.g., deposition or diffusion bonding processes) under conditions relevant to wear and friction (potentially including elevated temperatures and mechanical stresses).

decision.trend: Earlier works have increasingly focused on depositing high entropy alloy (HEA) films for wear‐resistant applications using advanced processing routes such as DC-magnetron sputtering. For example, one study deposited a Cu-containing refractory HEA film on substrates like silicon and stainless steel, showing that careful control over deposition temperature and subsequent annealing can yield a nanocrystalline structure with excellent wear properties and improved adhesion. However, these studies largely focused on substrates where chemical and thermal compatibility was less of an issue than with copper.
decision.unsolved: Despite the success in depositing wear-resistant HEA coatings, the challenge of achieving robust adhesion on a Cu matrix remains unsolved. This is due to the inherent differences in crystal structure, thermal expansion, and chemical affinity between copper and typical HEAs, which can lead to poor interfacial bonding and eventual delamination under service conditions.
decision.lever: Implementation of an engineered, graded interlayer at the Cu/HEA interface
decision.why: Based on the trend of using tailored deposition and post-treatment methods to improve film adhesion, the next plausible step is to develop a surface or interface engineering strategy. Specifically, designing a graded transition layer (potentially by incorporating a fraction of Cu into the HEA or by depositing an intermediate alloy with intermediate thermal expansion and chemical properties) is expected to enhance chemical and structural compatibility between the HEA coating and the copper substrate. This approach directly addresses the adhesion challenge dictated by the mismatch between Cu and a conventional high entropy alloy.
